items.title: 54270_Doc Cheatham oral history interview
items.q: Even Benny Carter, Benny Carter and I were great friends, you know, and I think I was responsible for Benny Carter taking up trumpet. I gave him his first mouthpiece.

ctx.x: I see so you joined him in 1940, but you -- you were still with him in April?

Yes, we didn't stay too long up there with the band, because the work was very -- you know at that time they would like hire one week-end then maybe after a couple of weeks, we'd go up there for another couple days, something like that, because it wasn't regular. They didn't keep any band up there, that type, you know, any length of time. Cause they were more interested in bands like the Savoy Sultans, they stayed up there, because the people were jumping more to that type of band, than they were Benny Carter's…
So they liked a band like the Sultans and Erskine Hawkins, type of band came and stayed there.

items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I had a job at the Empire Ballroom with my orchestra, and I managed to get Doc Cheatham to play with me in that orchestra.

ctx.x: Yes, because Doc Cheatham was in the orchestra with McKinney’s, wasn’t he?

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: And I just played with him up at Monterey -- the Monterey Festival.

ctx.x: Always the hard way. Just like with the trumpet. You know, I took it home and I thought I was gonna be an instant Cuban Bennett, you know, and then another name that I got to throw in here -- maybe it might be a little early -- but was a man whom I hadn't been influenced greatly yet, but was Doc Cheatham.

items.title: Doc Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 28, 1995
items.q: performing with the big bands of Cab Calloway, Teddy Wilson, Benny Carter and Chick Webb.

ctx.x: And that’s how I got Benny Goodman — before that I was with Benny Goodman. I played two years with him. We went to Las Vegas and other places. He played with symphonies sometimes and played jazz after that with his sextet. And he was very good to me. He fired everybody in the band at one time but myself. Because you know people don’t understand the man’s a genius, and he expected his men to play as well as he played. He expected that. And if you can’t satisfy him, you have to leave that’s all there is to it. And…

rehearse this, or what do you want to do fellas, you don’t do that. He just took his clarinet and played the [humms] played the melody and everything, and then he stopped all of a sudden, and started taking the clarinet apart and walking out. We said what’s wrong with this man? He walked out. And he stayed out [inaudible]. And so his valet came out and I said, “is this all?” He says, “yes, this is all.” He said, “don’t call me, we’ll call you” one of those things. So everybody started going out, packing up and…
